title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced one shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We revise methods and related-work presentation to (1) condense provenance into a compact archival pointer paragraph; (2) provide a single compact formal definition of the binary pass/fail scoring rule (with a concrete pass example drawn from archived scoring artifacts); and (3) add a nearest-work comparison matrix contrasting this paired shared-generation design with the closest prior executable-benchmark and repair studies. We discuss construct/external validity limits and give concrete design recommendations for follow-ups.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent into network configuration commands, promising productivity gains in NetOps. However, syntactically plausible command sequences can violate stateful workflow invariants (e.g., changing MTU without a required shutdown, unsafe uplink switchover), producing semantic failures only visible in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore advocates integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers to validate generated candidates before enactment. Evaluating guarded pipelines requires executable tests that detect sequencing and stateful violations beyond token or syntax checks.

We executed a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) to isolate the marginal effect of an executable validator and a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. The central confirmatory question: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To answer this, we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: each task produced one generator output that was scored both as baseline (LLM-only suggestion) and as guarded (validator ± repair). Holding the generator fixed removes generator-induced variability across paired episodes and directly measures the validator/repair subsystem's effect on identical candidates.

Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) holding the generator fixed; (2) complete execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation demonstrating adherence to the preregistered protocol; (3) a formal compact definition of the binary pass/fail scoring rule used in the confirmatory McNemar test and a concrete pass example from archived scoring artifacts; (4) a concise nearest-work comparison matrix that positions this shared-generation paired design relative to the closest executable-benchmark and repair studies; and (5) methodological recommendations for future confirmatory runs when generators rarely produce invalid candidates.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation-grounded benchmarks and NetOps verification tools emphasize that text-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment: closed-loop emulation exposes sequencing and stateful errors (make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, required-ordered operations) that syntactic checks miss. Tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) are repeatedly proposed as operational safety measures. Surveys and benchmark reports recommend integrating verification or emulation, but cross-model closed-loop comparisons under identical harnesses and experiments isolating validator effects are limited.

Nearest-work comparison (concise):
- Protogeros et al., "Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair" (arXiv:2604.22513): an executable benchmark and repair evaluation. Difference: prior work evaluates generator+repair behavior under standard benchmark protocols; our study isolates validator/repair marginal effect by using a shared initial generator output for paired scoring.
- NetConfArena (arXiv:2608.23179): an executable closed-loop benchmark for LLM agents. Difference: NetConfArena emphasizes multi-model agent evaluation; our contribution is a paired design that fixes the generator to measure validator/repair influence on identical candidates.
- MeshAgent (Zhou et al., 2025; DOI:10.1145/3771567): practical architectures for reliable LLM-based management. Difference: MeshAgent and similar system papers propose architectures and report improvement in practice; our experiment offers a preregistered paired statistical test that isolates the validator effect from generator variance.
- Lightyear (Tang et al., 2023; DOI:10.1145/3603269.3604842): modular verification for control-plane properties. Difference: Lightyear focuses on scaling verification engines; our work operationalizes a deterministic emulator validator in a paired design to measure repair impact on identical outputs.

This brief matrix highlights how prior executable evaluations and architectural proposals motivate but do not substitute for a paired shared-generation design that cleanly estimates the marginal utility of an executable validator plus bounded repair on the same generator outputs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) before execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary confirmatory design with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the prespecified test was the exact two-sided McNemar. A bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was included for the paired-difference estimate. The preregistration defined exclusion/contamination rules, a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), deterministic reset controls, and sensitivity analyses (e.g., counting technical exclusions as failures). The full preregistration identifier and hash are archived (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1; preregistration_sha256 recorded in the execution manifest).

Task generation, harness, and shared-generation design. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level). For each task we performed a single shared initial candidate generation using the declared model (gpt-5-mini). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}. This paired shared-candidate design isolates the marginal effect of the validator and repair subsystem by removing generator variance across paired episodes. The preregistration anticipated the risk that a well-calibrated generator on the chosen task bank could leave the repair subsystem idle.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable emulator/validator that checks task-encoded workflow policies (for example: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator executes the candidate in an emulated state checker and emits a structured validator_trace containing validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy invoked at most one repair iteration when validator.violation_count > 0; repair prompts and provider traces were archived when generated. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes and no repair artifacts were generated.

Compact provenance paragraph (condensed archival pointer). All primary execution and analysis artifacts are archived and checksummed in the manuscript evidence bundle. Representative artifact names include execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl; the execution and analysis manifests record SHA-256 summaries and reconciliations. Long provenance inventories previously shown inline have been condensed; full archived manifests and artifact lists are available in the evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration id (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) and by the execution manifest entries. (See Disclosure Statement for the immutable master-prompt reference and exact archival pointers.)

Formal binary scoring rule (compact, single definition). The confirmatory paired binary label Y_task ∈ {0,1} used for McNemar was derived deterministically from scoring/validator outputs as follows (applied to the episode-scoring JSON):
- Y_task = 1 (pass) iff scorer_id == "deterministic_netops_validator_v5" AND score == 1 AND scorer_score_reason == "VALID_CONFIGURATION" AND validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.violation_count == 0.
- Y_task = 0 (fail) otherwise (for example if score != 1, scorer_score_reason != "VALID_CONFIGURATION", or validator_trace.violation_count > 0).
This rule is the preregistered decision mapping from archived scorer/validator outputs to the paired binary outcomes used by the exact McNemar test.

Concrete pass example (archived artifact). Example drawn verbatim from execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (representative pair): normalized_response equals the normalized_reference_answer; score = 1; score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION"; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.violation_count = 0; validator_trace.repair_applied = false. Under the rule above, Y_pair-000001 = 1. No fail example exists in the archived run (validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes), so no recorded episode produced Y = 0 in this dataset.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Condition-level summaries record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0, guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes.

Per-topology outcomes. Deterministic partition produced 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology results (from the task manifest and scoring artifacts): Edge (40): baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Core (40): baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Leaf–spine (40): baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40. These counts are recorded in analysis/condition_summary.csv and representative scoring artifacts (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json).

Repair activity and secondary endpoints. Because validator.violation_count = 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied = false across the run and no repair_provider_trace artifacts exist. Preregistered secondary endpoints that quantify repair incidence are vacuous in this run; the absence of repair activity is an empirical observation recorded in validator traces and the execution manifest.

Contamination, missingness, and reconciliation. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero technical/instrumentation exclusions. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms provider-audit counts and pair accounting are internally consistent (n_11 = 120; hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The shared-generation paired design isolates the validator/repair subsystem's marginal effect by removing generator variance across paired episodes. In this archived task bank and with the declared generator/prompt configuration, the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling. This is an empirical outcome consistent with the preregistered design and archived artifacts (bootstrap seed/resamples and reconciliation files are available in analysis artifacts).

Design trade-offs and recommendations. The shared-generation protocol increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but may under-exercise repair when the generator is well-calibrated for the chosen task bank. Based on the archived task-manifest difficulty metadata and the recorded absence of repairs, we recommend the following preregistered adjustments for future confirmatory runs intended to measure repair utility:
1) Independent-generation arm: allow separate generator draws per condition so guarded pipelines can intercept generator errors that arise from prompt or sampling variability; preserve blocking or stratification to control confounds.
2) Targeted task selection: focus confirmatory power on tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count to increase the probability of generator-induced violations.
3) Controlled prompt perturbations: prespecify perturbations (exploratory in the original plan) on a subset to increase generator error incidence while retaining paired checks for other blocks.
4) Expanded repair budget: in exploratory arms allow multiple repair iterations to measure repair convergence and cost.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator's policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; while required_sequence enforces canonical workflows, the validator does not emulate every vendor-specific behavior or partial-observability telemetry. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation assumed baseline failure ≈ 0.40 and targeted an absolute reduction of 0.15; observed baseline = 0.00 violates those assumptions and renders the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.

Operational implications. Even when unused, an executable validator that emits structured traces (checked rules, touched fields, reasons repair was not applied) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. The archived artifacts demonstrate end-to-end instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, scoring traces, deterministic reconciliation) that can be repurposed for operator-facing explanations and third-party audits in deployments where generators sometimes err. The experiment emphasizes that claims about repair benefits require careful experimental framing: if generators rarely produce invalid candidates under a given prompt, the guard will be idle by design.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with one hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and shows that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts enable follow-ups that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
